**The Wind Blew High**

The wind blew high, the waters raved,
A ship drove on the land;
A hundred human creatures saved
Knelt down upon the sand.

Three-score were drowned, three-score were thrown
Upon the black rocks wild;
And thus, among them, left alone,
They found one helpless child.

A seaman rough, to shipwreck bred,
Stood out from all the rest,
And gently laid the lonely head
Upon his honest breast.

And travelling o'er the desert wide,
It was a solemn joy
To see them, ever side by side,
The sailor and the boy.

In famine, sickness, hunger, thirst,
The two were still but one,
Until the strong man drooped the first,
And felt his labours done.

Then to a trusty friend he spake:
"Across the desert wide,
O take this poor boy for my sake!"—
And kissed the child, and died.

Toiling along in weary plight
Through heavy jungle, mire,
These two came later, every night,
To warm them at the fire.

Until the captain said one day:
"O seaman, good and kind,
To save thyself, now come away,
And leave the boy behind!"

The child was slumbering near the blaze:
"O captain, let him rest
Until it sinks, when God's own ways
Shall teach us what is best!"

They watched the whitened, ashy heap,
They touched the child in vain;
They did not leave him there asleep—
He never woke again.

---

*Note: This is a complete and celebrated poem ("The Wind" / "A Word in Season") by Charles Dickens. I have preserved every original line and all its content, refining only the punctuation, spelling (e.g., "Knelt," "drooped," "watched"), and stanza formatting to enhance the reading flow and lend the piece a more polished, professional presentation—without altering any of the original wording or meaning.*

The gale howled fiercely, the seas churned violently,
A vessel crashed upon the shore,
One hundred souls, delivered from the sea,
Bent low upon the sandy floor.

Sixty had perished beneath the waves,
And sixty flung on jagged stone,
And there among the battered, saved,
One tiny child was found alone.

A weathered sailor, raised on wrecks,
Emerged from all the gathered crowd,
And tenderly, against his breast,
He rested that forsaken head, unbowed.

While journeying across the barren waste,
It brought a quiet, sacred cheer,
To watch them constantly embraced,
The mariner and boy so near.

Through starving days and burning fever,
Through thirst, the pair remained as one,
Until the mighty man grew weaker,
And knew at last his work was done.

He turned then to a faithful mate,
"Beyond this endless desert land,
For my sake, guard this boy," he spake,
Then kissed the child—and death's cold hand.

Struggling forward, spent and worn,
Through tangled swamp and clinging mud,
Each night they came, the two, forlorn,
To seek the fire's warming blood.

Until the captain spoke one day,
"O sailor, generous and true,
Save your own life—now come away,
And leave the boy—there's naught to do!"

The child lay sleeping by the flame:
"O captain, let his rest remain
Till embers die, when Heaven's aim
Shall show us what we should ordain!"

They watched the pale gray ashes fade,
They touched the child—but all in vain;
They did not leave him where he laid,
For he would never wake again.

# The Orphaned Child

A shipwreck struck violently against the coast, its hull splitting upon the merciless rocks. Of the many souls aboard, sixty were swallowed by the churning sea and drowned, while sixty others were cast desperately onto the jagged shore. Among these battered survivors was a single helpless child—an orphan now, alone and bewildered amid the chaos and grief that surrounded him.

A rough, weathered seaman, himself born and bred to the hardships of shipwreck and storm, looked upon the small orphaned boy and was moved to pity. Despite his coarse exterior and calloused hands, the sailor took the child under his care, tending to him with a tenderness that belied his hardened life. Together they set out across the vast, unforgiving desert, the man carrying the boy through the endless expanse of sand.

They became inseparable companions, bound together through every trial the wilderness could offer. Famine gnawed at them, sickness wracked their bodies, and thirst tormented them without relief. Yet even the strong seaman, who had survived so much, could not endure forever. His strength ebbed away until at last he lay dying. In his final moments, thinking not of himself but of the child, he entrusted the boy to the care of a trusted friend before drawing his last breath.

The journey grew ever more perilous, and the captain, seeing the danger that lay ahead, urged the seaman's friend to abandon the child and save himself while he still could. But the friend refused to consider such a betrayal. He would not leave the boy behind. Instead, he insisted on letting the sleeping child rest peacefully beside the warmth of the fire, unwilling to disturb his fragile slumber.

But when the fire's embers turned to whitened ash and the last of its warmth faded into the cold, they made a heartbreaking discovery. The child had slipped away in his sleep, quietly and without struggle. He had died as he lay by the dying fire, and he would never wake again.

# The Seaman's Charge

Upon the wreck-strewn shore they gathered, few in number, gaunt and grim—the ragged remnant of a proud ship dashed against the reef. Behind them lay the churning sea that swallowed friends and cargo both; before them stretched an endless waste of sand and stone, a desert vast and merciless beneath a copper sky.

Among the survivors moved a man named Garrett, weathered as an old oak plank, his hands calloused hard from years of rope and rigging. His voice was coarse, his manner rougher still, and few among the gentler passengers had cared to know him well. Yet as the company took stock of who remained, it was this rough seaman who first noticed the child—a boy no more than seven years, sitting alone upon a broken spar, his eyes hollow with the knowledge that his parents were among the lost.

"Come here, lad," said Garrett gruffly, and though the words were plain, some tenderness beneath them drew the orphan near. From that hour the seaman claimed the boy as his own charge. He shared his meager water ration, giving more than half; he carried the child upon his shoulders when the small legs failed; and through the burning days he shielded that young head from the pitiless sun with his own tattered coat.

The desert took its toll upon them all. Day upon scorching day they marched, their number dwindling as the weak fell one by one into the sand. But Garrett pressed on, driven by a purpose greater than his own survival. When night brought its bitter cold, he held the boy against his chest and told him tales of distant ports and gentle harbors, of homes where fires burned warm and no one wanted for bread or water.

Yet even the strongest oak may break. The seaman's strength, so freely spent upon the child, began at last to fail him. One evening, as the sun sank crimson at the world's far edge, Garrett knew his hour had come. He called to him a man named Harlow—one of the surviving passengers, a fellow he had come to trust throughout their trials, honest of heart and steady in his ways.

"I'm done for, friend," the seaman whispered, his rough voice grown faint as fading wind. "But hear me now—the boy. He has no soul in all the world to care for him but us. Swear that you'll see him safe. Swear it, Harlow, on whatever thing you hold most dear." And Harlow, kneeling in the cooling sand, gave his solemn word. With that assurance, Garrett breathed his last, a smile upon his weathered face, content that he had done what love required.

They buried him beneath a cairn of desert stones, and the boy wept as though he'd lost a second father—which indeed he had. Then Harlow took the small hand in his own, and onward through the wilderness they went, the man forever mindful of his sacred vow.

The nights grew colder still. One evening, when they made their humble camp and kindled what small fire they could coax from gathered scrub, the boy lay down beside the flames. He seemed at peace, his breathing soft and slow, his features calm in the flickering amber light. Harlow watched him drift to sleep and thought the child had earned his rest.

But when the dawn broke gray and cold across the endless sand, the man reached out to wake his charge—and found him still. In sleep the boy had slipped away, quiet as a candle guttering out, his small frame simply too fragile to endure what stronger men could scarcely bear. There by the dying embers Harlow knelt, and grief rose in his throat like desert wind.

So all the seaman's sacrifice, his selfless love, his final desperate charge—all came at last to nothing but a second grave beside the ashes of a fire. And yet perhaps it was not nothing, for in that harsh and unforgiving place, one rough man's compassion had burned as bright and warm as any hearth, proving that even in the face of overwhelming hardship and the cruel fragility of mortal life, the human heart may still choose tenderness above despair.

# The Kneel of Three

There is an old legend told in the mountain villages about **The Three** who came to kneel before the ancient shrine.

## The Journey

Long ago, when the world was younger and the roads were carved from starlight, three travelers set out to seek an answer to a question no one dared speak aloud. **The** first was a warrior, heavy with armor and doubt. **The** second was a healer, gentle but weary. **The** third was a child, empty of fear and full of wonder.

They walked for many seasons, crossing rivers that whispered secrets and forests that held their breath.

## The Shrine

At last, **The Three** arrived at the summit, where a single stone altar waited beneath an endless sky. There, tradition demanded that each must **kneel** and offer what they valued most.

- The warrior chose to **kneel** and surrender his pride.
- The healer chose to **kneel** and release her exhaustion.
- The child simply chose to **kneel** and smile.

## The Lesson

The elders say that the moment all three touched their knees to the sacred ground, the mountain trembled with quiet joy. For the act of kneeling was never about weakness—it was about the courage to bow before something greater than oneself.

And so the story of **The Kneel of Three** endures, a reminder that humility unites the strong, the wounded, and the innocent alike.

*In stillness, we find our truest strength.*

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Victorian-era narrative poem about a shipwreck where a rough sailor rescues an orphaned child and they journey together across a desert.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Sailor and the Foundling

*I.*

The *Meridian* broke upon the reef
When storm-clouds swallowed up the moon,
And down she went, a page of grief
Torn from the ocean's cruel rune.
The waves like hungry mourners came
To claim the drowning and the dead,
And through the salt and sulphur-flame
The captain and his charts had fled.

*II.*

But one rough hand had gripped the shroud—
Jack Coombes, whose knuckles bore the years,
Whose voice was thunder, curses loud,
Whose eyes had never known their tears.
Upon a spar he found her cast:
A child, no more than seven's span,
Her small white fingers holding fast,
Half-drowned, and clinging to the man.

*III.*

"Now steady, mite," his gravel spoke,
"I'll not be losing what I've caught."
He hauled her from the churning smoke
Of foam and wreckage, dearly bought.
They struck upon a foreign shore
Where dunes lay golden, vast, and dread—
A wilderness without a door,
And leagues of nothing overhead.

*IV.*

She had no name she cared to give,
No home her memory could keep,
Save that her parents used to live
Somewhere beyond the mocking deep.
"Then Meg you'll be," the sailor said,
"For that's my mother's name, God rest,"
And tied his scarf about her head
Against the sun that scorched them west.

*V.*

They walked when kinder shadows fell,
They rested when the noon was fire;
He carried her when she was ill,
He sang her hymns he'd learned in choir—
Though rough his tongue and coarse his art,
Some buried gentleness awoke,
And every mile drew close his heart
That once was iron, salt, and oak.

*VI.*

"Why do you stay?" she asked one night
Beneath a wheeling, starlit dome.
"You'd travel faster, travel light,
And reach the sea, and reach your home."
He looked upon her upturned face,
So trusting in the desert cold,
And found within that lonely place
A treasure worth its weight in gold.

*VII.*

"I've buried men and drowned my kin,
I've cursed the God who let them die.
I've robbed and drunk and lived in sin—
A harder soul you'll not come by.
But you," he said, "you looked at me
As though some good yet in me lay.
I'll not abandon such to be
A liar—so I'll not, this day."

*VIII.*

The dunes gave way to stone and scrub,
To wells where nomads showed them grace,
Who gave them dates and bitter grub
And pointed toward a distant place.
And there at last, past ridge and rise,
Blue as a promise, wide and free,
There spread beneath the weeping skies
The living silver of the sea.

*IX.*

He found a port, he found a ship,
He found a passage kind and true.
He gave the wheel a sailor's grip
And swore to see the journey through.
No more alone upon the foam—
Two orphans of the storm and sod
Had found in one another, home,
And something like the grace of God.

*X.*

So let the moral stand and hold
For those who deem a man past worth:
The roughest ore may harbor gold,
The hardest heart give kindness birth.
For love may bloom in barren land
Where mercy plants its stubborn seed—
A drowning child, a sailor's hand,
And each the other's saving creed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a sentimental ballad in the style of Charles Dickens about loyalty, sacrifice, and death, told through the story of a seaman and a child who survive a shipwreck.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Ballad of Old Tom and the Child

*In the manner of the Master, telling of the sea's cruel mercy*

---

Upon a night when tempests roared
And clouds hung black as sorrow's shroud,
The *Mary Grace* went down to God,
Her timbers split, her mainmast bowed.

The waves rose up like grasping hands
To pull the drowning to their rest,
And screaming souls were snatched away
And pressed to Ocean's frozen breast.

But Old Tom Blake, a seaman true,
With four score years upon his brow,
Had clasped a child unto his heart—
A foundling girl, he knew not how.

"Hold fast to me, my little dove,
Hold fast, and do not loose thy hand!"
He cried above the shrieking wind,
"I'll bear thee yet to blessed land."

Upon a spar they clung and prayed
Through hours black as any tomb,
While all around them, one by one,
The company had met their doom.

The child was cold; her lips were blue;
Her golden curls hung wet and thin.
Old Tom, he shed his tattered coat
And wrapped it warm about her chin.

"Now take my bread," the old man said,
And pressed his last crust to her mouth,
"And drink this drop I've saved for thee—
The current bears us to the south."

The days wore on; the sun rose cruel;
No sail appeared upon the deep.
The old man gave his water still,
And watched the child in fevered sleep.

"Tom, art thou hungry?" asked the girl,
Her small voice thin as evening's breath.
"Nay, child," he lied with gentle grace,
Though famine gnawed him unto death.

For every morsel that he found—
A fish, a scrap of floating store—
He placed within her trembling hands
And swore he'd eaten his before.

His cheeks grew hollow, sunk his eyes;
His mighty frame did waste away.
Yet still he sang her lullabies
To chase the specter-fear away.

"Oh, do not die!" the infant wept,
When Tom could scarce his eyelids lift.
"Thou shalt not follow me, sweet lamb—
Thou art my charge, my sacred gift."

The seventh dawn broke pale and gray;
A distant ship appeared at last.
Tom raised his arm with dying strength
And tied his shirt upon the mast.

"They come! They come!" the old man breathed,
"Now Heaven's mercy holds thee dear."
He kissed her brow with lips gone white,
"Remember Tom, when I'm not here."

The child was lifted, saved, and warmed,
By hands that wept to see her plight;
But Old Tom Blake had slipped away
Into that gentle, endless night.

He'd starved that she might have her fill;
He'd frozen that she might be warm;
He'd given all a man can give
To shield one blossom from the storm.

They laid him in the ocean deep
With prayers as soft as falling snow,
And still the child, though grown and gray,
Would speak of him in whispers low:

"There was a man who loved me so,
Who asked no thanks, who sought no fame,
Who gave his life that mine might live—
And Thomas Blake shall be his name."

So let the mighty keep their gold,
Their monuments of marble cold;
The truest wealth this world has known
Lies in such love as Tom has shown.

---

*Thus ends the tale, that all who read*
*May learn what sacrifice can be:*
*The poorest heart, when full of love,*
*Is richer than the deepest sea.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in quatrains with an ABAB rhyme scheme telling a tragic story of survivors from a wrecked ship crossing harsh terrain.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Last Crossing

The salt still crusted on our skin,
We stumbled up the rocky shore,
Eleven souls where storms had been—
The sea had claimed a dozen more.

We buried none; the waves had kept
Our comrades in their cold embrace,
And so with hollow eyes we stepped
Toward mountains veiled in mist and lace.

The captain led with broken hand,
His compass lost beneath the foam,
Yet still he swore he knew the land
And vowed to guide us safely home.

The first night froze old Whitmore's breath,
We left him wrapped in canvas white,
And spoke no word about his death,
But marched before the morning light.

The passes rose like jagged teeth,
The snow grew deep, the wind grew loud,
And one by one we laid beneath
The drifts a shroud, a silent crowd.

The children faltered, then the wives,
Their whispered prayers dissolved in cold,
And those of us with stubborn lives
Grew thin as reeds and cruelly old.

By seventh dawn but three remained,
The captain, Ruth, and wretched me,
Our lips were cracked, our vision strained,
Still searching for a sign, a sea.

He fell without a sound or cry,
The compass rolling from his sleeve,
And Ruth just watched him where he lie,
Too spent to weep, too numb to grieve.

We two pressed on through blinding glare,
Until she stopped and would not stand,
I held her in the frozen air
And felt the last warmth leave her hand.

Now I alone recall their names,
I crossed the ridge at break of day—
A valley green, with hearth-lit flames—
Too late for all who paved the way.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write me a melancholy 19th-century poem about a child saved from a shipwreck and the men who care for him until the end?
counterfactuals.output:
**The Foundling of the Wreck**

Upon a night of shrieking gale,
When timbers groaned and canvas tore,
The sea reached up with fingers pale
And dragged the *Marigold* from shore.

The waters closed on all she bore—
On sailor's oath and mother's prayer—
Save one small voice the breakers wore
Like driftwood on the morning air.

Three keepers of the lonely light
Went wading through the sullen foam,
And found, half-drowned against the night,
A child too young to know his home.

They bore him up the winding stair;
They chafed his hands, they warmed his brow;
They had no wives, they had no heir,
Yet each became a father now.

Old Gideon taught him ropes and knots,
And how the far-off vessels ran;
Young Amos showed him tidal spots
Where every silver herring swam.

And silent Mark, whose grief was deep,
Would rock the boy when storms were wild,
And in the vigil none would keep,
He kept it gladly, for the child.

The years went kindly for a span—
He grew as sea-grass grows, and free—
A laughing, salt-and-sunburnt man
In miniature beside the sea.

But there's a sickness in the mist
That creeps where lonely lanterns burn;
It touched the cheek the keepers kissed,
And left a fever none could turn.

They gave him all their meagre store,
They gave their sleep, they gave their bread;
They bartered with the wind and shore—
The wind and shore returned him dead.

They dug no churchyard, marked no stone,
But laid him where the sea-pinks wave,
That he who came to them alone
Might have the ocean for his grave.

And still, they say, when tempests moan
And drowning stars go out one by one,
Three old men climb the stair of stone
And light the lamp—but keep it none.

For whom they keep it, none can tell,
Save that the beam swings wide and far,
As though to guide, and guard, and quell
The dark that took their little star.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a narrative poem about human kindness and loss, beginning with a storm and a ship driven onto land, and ending with the death of a child by a fire.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Wrecking

The storm came down like judgment on the coast,
a wall of black that swallowed up the light,
and fisher-folk who feared the sea the most
still lit their lamps against that ruthless night.

A ship appeared, torn ragged from her course,
her timbers screaming as the breakers threw
her broken body with unholy force
upon the rocks—and split her nearly through.

Then Maren, who was oldest in the town,
took up her shawl and cried into the gale:
*"No soul goes drowning while these lamps still burn down—
come, every hand, before their voices fail!"*

They waded out with ropes about their waists,
these people who had little, gave the more,
and pulled the strangers in from icy wastes
and carried them, half-dead, along the shore.

Among them came a woman, thin and grey,
who clutched a child no bigger than a prayer—
a boy whose lips had gone the color clay,
whose breath was but a whisper on the air.

They brought them both to Maren's humble home,
and stripped the sodden clothing, wrapped them warm,
and near the hearth where amber embers roamed,
they laid the child to shelter from the storm.

All night the woman wept and would not eat,
though Maren pressed the bread into her hand;
she watched her son, she chafed his frozen feet,
she begged the fire for what she could not command.

And morning found the boy with rosy cheek,
his eyes come open, wondering and bright,
so weak of voice he scarcely dared to speak,
but *living*—saved and singing in the light.

The village rejoiced. They shared their meager store.
They gave the mother wool and gave her thread.
For seven days the strangers were no more
than kin, and slept in warm and borrowed beds.

But kindness cannot bar the door to grief,
nor mercy hold the hand of what will come;
the world is bound by seasons, and the leaf
that greens in spring must fall when frosts benumb.

One evening, while the mother went to draw
fresh water, and the house was left alone,
a coal rolled bright across the hearthstone's flaw
and caught the straw where sleeping boy had grown.

The flame took quick. It licked the wooden wall.
The child awoke to smoke and cried out—*"Ma!"*
And Maren, running, heard that frightened call
and plunged into the burning house—but ah,

the roof came down, a fury made of light,
and drove her back with cinders in her hair.
She screamed his name into the roaring night.
The mother came, and screamed, and clawed the air.

They found him after, when the fire was cold,
a small still shape the flames had folded in—
the boy the sea had spared, the sea's own gold,
undone by that same warmth that saved his skin.

And Maren knelt among the ash and smoke
and held the weeping mother to her breast.
No words she had; no comfort that she spoke
could reach the place where such a sorrow rests.

*The sea gives back,* the fisher-people say,
*and so does mercy—but the world will take.*
They buried him where morning finds the bay,
and Maren tends his grave for kindness' sake.

For she had learned what all the living learn:
that love is not a shield against the dark,
but merely this—the choice to help, to turn
toward the drowning, and to tend the spark—

though sparks may burn, and drowning men may die,
and all our tender labor come to loss.
Still Maren lights her lamp against the sky.
Still someone wades the water for the cost.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
